On the Orders of the Day:
Hon. GEORGE H. BOTVIN (Minister of Customs and Excise):	Mr. Speaker, before
the orders of the day are called I would like to say that on February 1 the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) asked if I would lay on the table all orders in council issued during the past two years for the release of alcohol from distilleries within a shorter period of time than that set forth in the Inland Revenue Act. I am glad now to be able to place these orders on the table of the House, together with a copy for my hon. friend.

The House resumed from Wednesday, February 3, consideration of the motion of Hon. Mr. Lapointe that when the House adjourns immediately after the conclusion of the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, it stand adjourned until March 15, 1926, and the amendment thereto of Hon. Mr. Stevens.

Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned yesterday I was referring to the supplementary address which had been presented to parliament by the Prime Minister on January 28, through the lips of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). Perhaps it would be well for 14011-47i
me to read this address which was presented on that occasion. It is as follows:
Ottawa, January 28, 1926.
J. S. Woodsworth, M.P.,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Woodsworth,
Replying to the letter received from Mr. Heaps and yourself, dated January 7, in which you ask whether it is the intention of the government to introduce at this session legislation with regard to
(a)	provision for the unemployed, and
(b)	old age pensions, I would refer you, respecting provision for the unemployed, to the answer given in the House of Commons to-day by the Hon. Ernest Lapointe on behalf of the government in reply to a question by yourself and which indicated the government's intention of carrying out with respect to emergency relief the practice adopted in co-operation with provinces and municipalities in the years immediately following the war. In answer to a question from Mr. Neill, Mr. Lapointe further intimated that it was the intention of the government to introduce at this session legislation with respect to Old Age Pensions. You will observe that the statement made by Mr. Lapointe was in accordance with the intimation which I gave to Mr. Heaps and yourself at the time of our interview, following the receipt of the communication herein referred to.
With respect to amendments to (a) the Immigration Act, (b) the Naturalization Act, and (c) the Criminal Code, which were referred to at the time of our interview, I would say that having since taken up the proposed amendments with the ministers concerned, I feel I am in a position to assure you that legislation on these matters will also be introduced in the course of the present session.
Yours sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King.
Prior to bringing this matter up I had been referring to the feeling which prevails in the country that a good deal of bargaining has been going on between the government and some of the groups in this House with a view to the continuation of the government in office. I referred to a Canadian Press report on that occasion, which was denied by the chief whip of the Progressive party and also by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell), which press report contained this statement:
The Progressive party will sell its support in the best interests of the west.
This statement was denied by those gentlemen, in so far as the word "sell" is concerned, and I accept their denial; I do not question their veracity at all. I have always had a good deal of respect for the hon. gentlemen who sit behind the leader of the Progressive party, and I am sorry that I am not able to say as much for their leader.	But there
is something further in that report which the hon. member for Mackenzie did not deny, and it is as follows:
What legislation it can secure in the interests of the west is the fundamental question that will decide its actions.

Apparently they have been satisfied in their demands, because the government have promised in the Speech from the Throne to introduce legislation-mark the words " introduce legislation ", perhaps not expecting it to pass- along the lines desired, although in years gone by the government had used their best endeavours to defeat such legislation. Apparently the leader of the so-called Labour group in the House became jealous of the influence which was being exercised by the Progressive party. Although he and his colleague had approached the Prime Minister and had received verbal assurance that their request would be complied with they were not satisfied, and1 insisted that before the next vote wag taken they should have a definite statement from the Prime Minister, over his own signature, as to what he would do under the circumstances. Is it any wonder that the people of this country have become alarmed, that the press of Canada is filled from day to day with references to the bargaining which it is claimed is going on in the House of Commons. At this point, in order to give still further point to my remarks, I might refer to my last few observations before the House rose at six o'clock last night. Referring to the letter from the Prime Minister to M!r. Woods-worth, I stated that it is:
-the clearest and most emphatic proof of the fact that there has been bargaining in relation to matters of great public importance in this country with a view to securing support in this House to enable a government which was defeated at the polls, to carry on in defiance of public opinion. And the government is now asking for a six weeks' adjournment in order to build up its shattered forces.
Those hon. members who were in the House yesterday and listened to the Minister of Justice will appreciate the situation more accurately when I read the words which the minister made use of on that occasion. He said:
Now, we are the government and we are only asking fair play, the same fair play that we should have been pleased to extend to my right hon. friend if he had been successful, and had carried a majority in this House. We desire an adjournment to permit the Prime Minister to undertake and to carry through the task of filling vacancies and to reconstruct the government in order to proceed regularly with the legislative, parliamentary and administrative work of government.
This is an admission on the part of the leader of the government that they are unable under present conditions to carry on. The importance therefore of having the representatives of groups in this House lend their support to the government will be appreciated. The Minister of Justice goes on to say:

-that the government should be complete and that every department should be represented here by a minister.
Now the Speech from the Throne contains the information that a number of departments are to be merged and certain ministers eliminated. What it is proposed to do has not been disclosed to the House but the leader of the government forces in the House, in his evident distress, pleads that it is necessary to have a minister here at the head of all departments of the government. I wonder if those hon. members sitting behind the government feel that some of the ministers defeated at the polls are better qualified than they are to take charge of and' administer departments. The Prime Minister himself was most decisively defeated in a constituency where he sought to test public opinion with respect to himself and his government. The defeat which he sustained on that occasion should be sufficient to convince him and his colleagues that the people have very little use for the man who has been leading the Liberal forces during the past few years. And remember M.r. King ran in a constituency where he is well known and is not a stranger as he is in the riding where he is now endeavouring to secure re-election. Perhaps I may be permitted to say here that the scolding, petulant mood exhibited by Mr. Mackenzie King before the electors of Prince Albert is by no means to his credit. "Why," he demands, "where does this young man who is my opponent come from? Who dares to put this man into the field in opposition to the great William Lyon Mackenzie King? The people of this country Should know who are at the back of this conspiracy Let me say that there is a band of men in Canada prepared to stand by the empire, a band prepared to make any sacrifice necessary to maintain that empire and to see that it is perpetuated. Is it surprising that one of those men who served in the ranks of the Canadian forces during the greatest crisis that this empire has ever faced, should now step forward and oppose even the self-styled great William Lyon Mackenzie King? The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) dealt with this point most effectively yesterday. I should have lost faith in our country had not someone at this period of national crisis been nominated to oppose this man. And now the government are asking parliament to adjourn until March 15 in order to enable him to build up his shattered forces, in order to secure the election of one William Lyon Mackenzie King. According to them it is their only hope. The shattered Liberal forces are looking for leader-

Adjournment-Customs Inquiry
ship, and the Minister of Justice makes the plaintive plea "Give us fair play. We would do the same to you under similar circumstances." Ah! has he forgotten the statements of this same William Lyon Mackenzie King with regard to the right hon. gentleman who leads the major group in this House after the general election of 1921 when the latter endeavoured to secure re-election in a constituency close by and where he was well known? Why there was on that occasion,
I might almost say, gross misrepresentation by the man who now claims to be Prime Minister, to say nothing of the same petulance which he is manifesting in the Prince Albert by-election. This ought to be a sufficient answer to the Minister of Justice. It indicates what hon. gentlemen opposite would do under similar circumstances.
As I have already said, the Speech from the Throne intimates that certain departments are to be merged. We do not know how many ministers will be seeking re-election, possibly not any outside of the Prime Minister. Then why this adjournment? Last night I quoted a statement from the Winnipeg Free Press published on the day following the general election. That journal anticipated that the only thing the Prime Minister could do under the circumstances was to send in his resignation, and recommend His Excellency to call upon the right hon. leader of the opposition to form a government. But the Prime Minister and his ministers decided not to do that, they determined to hang on to office let the consequences be what they would. But they did announce that parliament would be called at the earliest possible moment, and that it would assemble on December 10 in order to transact the business of the country. The date of the opening of parliament was afterwards changed to January 7. The House has now been in session for nearly a month, and it is quite evident that the administration admit their inability to carry on and despatch public business. The Speech from the Throne is absolutely at variance with the professions while in office of the leader of the party opposite and his government. I referred to those yesterday, and in particular to the question of the building of the Hudson Bay railway. On that occasion the Minister of Railways, the Right Hon. George P. Graham, made the statement that parliament as then constituted would not vote money for the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. At that time the Liberals had a following of 117 members in this House, and 63 or 64 members of the Progressive party were in the House
advocating the building of the road. But now, with their forces decimated, with their ranks depleted, there has apparently been an effort to get Progressive support. My hon. friends opposite say to them, "We will promise you members of the Progressive party anything, if you will only support us and enable us to carry on." Is it any wonder that the Progressives in this House have absolutely no confidence in the King government? They have good reason not to have any confidence in it. They realize to-day that the government is dependent upon them in order to enable it to carry on. The government must now concede everything that the Progressives ask in order to secure their support. I have altogether too high a regard for my hon. friends of the Progressive party to think that they have any faith in a government which is forced under such circumstances to grant such concessions in order to secure their support so that the government may be enabled to hang on to office. 'Surely there is something higher and nobler in public life than merely to hold on to office.
But the most significant, yes, the most amusing thing that has happened in this House in many years was the introduction of the .motion to adjourn parliament for six weeks, or until the 15th day of March, without any explanation from the leader of the government as to why this should be done-not a word. The motion came before the House and the debate began without any attempt to justify it. We had no explanation to warrant such action, although a number of the members were here in the House, until yesterday when the acting leader of the government (Mr. Lapointe) rose and made his plea. He found fault with hon. members on this side of the House for depriving him of an opportunity to speak when the motion was introduced. I do not think a more-I will not say ridiculous, but unusual claim, was ever before advanced; because it is well known that the hon. leader of the House had a perfect right to speak on the motion, and should have done so. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) would gladly have given way to him had he shown any evidence of a desire to speak on that occasion. After the debate had continued for some time he took the floor and made the plea, "Oh, give us fair play; do not embarrass us in our distress. We are anxious to serve our country and1 are particularly anxious to carry on the government. We do not like to go out into the cold shades of opposition."
It was rather significant that this motion was sprung in the House on the 2nd day of

Adjournment - -Casio,ns Inquiry
February. Hon. members know that there is an old adage that the bear, who has a habit of going into a warm place and hibernating during the winter, on the 2nd day of February comes out and surveys his surroundings, and if the sun is shining brightly he concludes there are to be six weeks more of winter and he immediately goes back to stay in his nest for another six weeks. That is what the government are doing. When they found that on the 2nd of February the sun was shining brightly all day long, and there was every prospect of storm and stormy weather for the next six weeks, they said1 to us, '"Now if you fellows will only go home for six weeks and wait until the spring arrives, we .will then take up again the business of the country."
This appeal was followed! by an address by my good friend the Minister of Finance. What was his plea? We would expect from him some good1 sound argument which would appeal to the judgment of members of this House as to why an adjournment should be granted. Did he favour us with such an argument? I listened to his remarks and I looked over Hansard this morning, and I cannot see that he has done so; but he attempted to belittle the charges which were made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), the most serious charges that were ever preferred against a government in Canada. Did he deal with those? Well, in his own way he did. He says, "It is quite true that the bootleggers are a very strong force in this country at the present time. Parliament voted $350,000 a year ago to suppress smuggling and bootlegging and things of that kind, but the government are absolutely helpless. The automobile enables these men to frustrate the efforts of the government." I could not help thinking what a force the government could have let loose on the country if they had only manned the automobiles which they have at their command. But only some $23,100 of that $350,000 vote was used *for this purpose.
The Minister of Finance says, "Why, these bootleggers from Montreal endeavoured to defeat me in my election," and he attempted to connect them with the Tory organization in the city of Montreal. I am glad to hear that there is a Tory organization in the city of Montreal; I was not aware of it before. The effect of the bootleggers' assistance so far as the Tory party was concerned in the province of Quebec was not anything to boast about, but I recall the fact that while the Minister of Finance was a candidate in his own constituency there were other candidates

who had other difficulties to contend with. I remember the election very well, and I think I will remember it for some time. I am sorry that the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) is not in his seat. In view of the fact that the Minister of Finance introduced this matter, I think I am justified in relating some of the things which took place in other constituencies. We remember that in the last session of this parliament-indeed it has been brought up every session-a proposal urged and agitated by hon. members to my left, with the supposed endorsation of the government, namely, what is known as the transferable vote in single member constituencies. But no measure to that end was put into effect. In fact the bill was not introduced by the government, although it remained on the order paper until the last day of the session. But in the recent election they adopted an entirely new system. Notwithstanding the fact that they had 83,000 election agents paid out of the public treasury of the country during the last election, they put into effect a brand new system-not the transferable vote in single member constituencies, but t'he transferring of the voters themselves bodily into other constituencies with a view of assisting the government in their distress. I am fully conscious of the responsibility of a member of parliament in making statements on the floor of this House. It is true that very often recldess statements are indulged in by some speakers at the time of an election, but when we are in the parliament hon. members should be careful what they say. I have made the statement that the government adopted a different system; in view of the fact that the transferable vote in single member constituencies did not go into effect they transferred the voters bodily from one constituency to another, in fact from one province to another.
I see some of my hon. friends from Quebec looking very intently at me, as though I was making a rather reckless statement. They may be surprised to know that a carload of the residents of Quebec were brought into the constituency of South Oxford and that deliberate attempts were made to put those men on the voters' list in that constituency. After failing in several attempts they succeeded in getting at least seven of them on the list in one polling division of that constituency. It was only on the day of nomination. when the registrar for that constituency handed in his list of names which had been added by him, that I ascertained that these men's names had been placed on the voters' list. Perhaps I had better make clear the extent to which I realized the need for caution,

Adjournment-Customs Inquiry
the need for watching closely what was going on. On the 19th of October I had published in the press of the constituency a notice to this effect:
Warning
To the returning officer and registrars appointed to make up the voters' lists in South Oxford.
I have personal knowledge of the fact that names are being placed on the voters' lists for this election in South Oxford by registrars in the rural districts, of persons who are not only not entitled to have their names on the list, but who have already had then-names registered as voters in other parts of this constituency-
I have affidavits to that effect and I can prove it before the Committee on Privileges and Elections when it is appointed.
-and are therefore guilty of the offence of personation, the penalty for which offence as a fine of $2,000 or a term of imprisonment of two years.
I have	been	informed by	one of the	registrarsappointed	that	these names	were added	with theknowledge	and	consent oif the returning	officer. I
have since confirmed this by telephone conversation with the returning office.
As the	time	[DOT]for revising	these lists will expire
to-morrow, October 20, at six o'clock p.m.
I herewith issue this warning to the returning officer and to all registrars for this constituency fto take immediate action to have the voters' lists made up according to the regulations contained in the Dominion Elections Act.
Unless this is done, action will be taken against all who have violated their oath of office and also against those guilty of the offence lot personation.
What happened then? An editor from western Canada, a man who had resided there for many years, was sent into the constituency, and he edited a full page in one of the local papers day after day. "Oh," he taunted, "this is an election bluff; the candidate has nothing to substantiate anything of that kind." What happened? I immediately took steps to see that these people who had been transported from another province into the constituency of South Oxford would not vote there in that election. As a result, a warrant was issued by the crown to arrest the leader of the party who was responsible for adding these names. Who do you suppose it turned out to be? One of this army of 83,000 agents appointed by the government, one of their deputy returning officers. Is it any wonder that they are asking parliament to adjourn for six weeks in order to bolster up their shattered forces? This man was arrested by the crown when I informed the authorities what had happened and gave them the evidence to substantiate it. He was let out on bail, brought before a magistrate and convicted of perjury. This was one of the election officers to whom I had referred in the warning which I had caused to be published a few days previously.
Others from western Canada were also very active in the campaign in that constituency, but I need not refer to more than two or three of them. They were men who had been associated with the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) for many years, men who had first been elected to the legislature of Alberta in the same year that the Minister of the Interior was elected, one of whom had drawn $19,900 odd out of the treasury of this country while he was an organizer for the Liberal party and who was eventually forced off the payroll. I warned the government time and again with regard to what was going on, and one of the most disgraceful scenes that I ever witnessed in parliament took place when I was prevented from discussing the matter on the floor of this House. One of the ministers who was responsible for blocking that discussion is no longer in parliament. This man, so far as I know, is now off the payroll. He was appointed organizer for Ontario on behalf of the Liberal government. Time and again he came into the constituency to secure a candidate so as to link up in some way the Progressives or the United Farmers of Ontario, as we call them, and the Liberal party in South Oxford. Finally he succeeded in doing that to his satisfaction by getting the executives of the two parties to meet together in a little hall after dark in a most obscure place in the constituency. They decided that they would coordinate. That is the word they are frequently using; they speak of the need of coordination or co-operation. Having succeeded in this, they secured a man who for years had been very active as a member of the United Farmers of Ontario, or as a Progressive and had opposed the Liberal party. But they decided that the Liberal party would nominate this man as their candidate and that the Progressive party would work behind him, and in that way they hoped to defeat the candidate on behalf of the opposition. This worked out all right for a little while. The elections came on and everything was going fine. The editor from western Canada who was editing this page in a local paper loaded' it up from day to day with the most ridiculous statements that were ever advanced in any election, until finally another ex-member of the government of Alberta arrived to bolster up the forces. I do not like to refer to this gentleman today, because I believe he is now being tried at Edmonton for the alleged offence of looting the treasury of that province. But this is what happened, and these are some of the things which I had to contend with in the

last election. I am not surprised that the Minister of Finance has gone out of the chamber. He has heard enough; he is already convinced that his complaint about bootleggers operating in his constituency on behalf of the Conservative party has paled into insignificance as compared with what has been going on in some other parts of the country. Yes, Mr. Duncan Marshall, organizer for the Liberal party, and Mr. George Peter Sinith, were colleagues of the Minister of the Interior until 1921 when they were turned out of office by the people of the province of Alberta. The people of Alberta evidently were heartily sick and tired of that government, but they were not content to retire to private life. From day to day the gallery of this House has been, I will not say adorned, but at any rate occupied by a man who has been active, if not in the public life of this country, at least behind the scenes with the Liberal party in Canada for many years. I referred to this matter last session on several occasions, as the Minister of Justice will recall, at the time the Petersen contract was before parliament. I referred to the author, the man who was responsible for making the contract and who was directing and advising the government in the matter of that contract. He was going to save Canada, so he claimed, from the great octopus which was draining the life blood of the farmers of the west, and in fact of Canada as a whole. The government, we were given to understand, were by this scheme to break up the North Atlantic shipping combine, although the government had the Canadian Government Merchant Marine in it.
Now it is rather significant that for many years, as far back at least as I can recall, this man has been an active agent of the Liberal party in Ontario and in the Dominion of Canada. In 1,903 or 1904 the Patrons of Industry were organized in Ontario, and it is just as well for us to understand that these farmers' organizations do not spring into existence altogether from any desire on the part of the farmers to participate in politics; there is a much felt need among those engaged in agriculture to organize with a view to legitimately furthering their interests. At that time the author of the Petersen contract was the organizer for the Liberal party in the province of Ontario.

I rise to a point
of order. I have listened with a good deal of deference to my hon. friend but I am utterly unable to see what the Petersen contract has to do with the resolution before the House and the amendment thereto.

I
always like to give way to any reasonable request, but it is not my fault if the hon. gentleman is unable to see the connection. Now the person to whom I was referring-
I ask, Mr. Speaker, for a decision on the point of order.

Hon. members taking
part in a debate should adhere as closely as possible to the subject matter of the discussion. I presume that the hon. member (Mr. Sutherland, South Oxford) will bring the present trend of his remarks to bear on the motion before the Chair, and before ruling on the point of order I shall wait a reasonable time until he does so.

I
am perfectly satisfied that Your Honour will see the relevancy of my remarks in this connection to the motion before the House. If the hon. member for Joliette does not see it it is not my fault, but I assure you, Sir, that I shall be able to connect the Petersen contract with the present situation and particularly with the motion under consideration. I shall show why this House should not adjourn for six weeks in order to enable a discredited party to carry on, with certain officials in the gallery of this House directing their policy. The Prime Minister cannot come in and take a seat in this House but has been dodging around the corridors since parliament met, until a week ago. He is now in the constituency of Prince Albert whining about having as opposition a young man there who is he claims going to lose his $200 deposit because he presumes to oppose the great Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my remarks last night, as it is to-day, is to show the connection between the feeling which prevails in this country, in regard to the bargaining that has been going on for support in this House, and the situation as we have it at the present time; and I am going back a few years to prove that this connection has been maintained right along and is being kept up to-day by the agents of the Liberal party who were operating in the province of Ontario a few years ago. The matter was referred to last night by several speakers. In 1893 and 1884, Mr. W. T. R. Preston was the paid organizer of the Liberal party in Ontario and in the same years Mr. Duncan Marshall was the paid organizer of the Patrons of Industry in that province. These associations continued for a number of years until the final merging process took place about the year

Adjournment-Customs Inquiry
1898, and it is significant that these are the men who were directing operations in the recent election in the endeavour to merge the Liberal party with a farmers' organization which was originally created and intended to serve a useful purpose. After this amalgamation had been accomplished in 1898, the organizer for the Patrons of Industry, Mr. Duncan Marshall, ran as a straight Liberal candidate in the constituency of Muskoka, where he was decisively defeated and rejected. He then went out to the west where he Succeeded in getting a foothold in the legislature of Alberta, where he represented the smallest constituency in that province. I do not think that there were ever so few people who had a representative in a legislature. After all these years, after being turned out of office, he was found sitting the morning after the election of 1921 on the door-step of the Minister of Agriculture, whom he was asking to take care of him. The minister did so, and when the vote to provide for him was before the House, referred to him as "my special messenger, Mr. Duncan Marshall." When this man was directing operations in Ontario a carload of people were brought into South Oxford, residents of the province of Quebec, and some of them put on the voters' list there. Reference has been made to perjury committed in this connection: it was only by the adoption of heroic measures and the arrest of the ringleader of the gang that we succeeded in putting a little scare into them. Had that not been the case I do not know how far they would have gone. I have considerable faith in the people of my constituency, and when they realized what was going on there was a revulsion of feeling which was unmistakable. The methods that had been adopted in that election were resented.
Now what I have been saying leads up to one of my objections to the adjournment of parliament. I made representations to the chief electoral officer and I noticed that the statutory report of that officer has been tabled in the House. I am curious to know what is contained in that report. A most unusual thing happened. After I had reported to the chief electoral officer he communicated with the returning officer, and in a long letter covering Several pages he complained about my attitude in taking exception to certain things. Some of the deputy returning officers had failed to comply with the act, had in fact absolutely disregarded it to such an extent that, when the official count took place, in several polls we were not able to find a statement as to the result of the poll. This letter,
I was informed, had been received from the returning officer. Immediately I wrote back and pointed out that his attempt to justify and exonerate the man who had been convicted of perjury was sufficient evidence to show that he was absolutely unfit for the position which he held. He referred to the evidence which had been given by one of his deputies as being very straight evidence. This party was not called at all; he was being tried on a criminal charge. His counsel knew better than to place him in the witness box; the crown could not do so. After he had been found guilty of perjury I did something that I had no right to do. The crown attorney beckoned to me. I went over to him and said that so far as I was concerned I hoped that the young man would not be sent to prison. He was let out on suspended sentence by the magistrate. The fact that he was so discharged is being held up by the returning officer-and I am afraid that it will appear in the report which has been presented to parliament-as evidence that his offence was not very serious. As is well known, in a case of conviction for perjury there is no option to impose a fine; the one convicted must be sent to prison. It is most significant that a few years ago this young man lost his position a3 telegraph operator for forging a pass. I did not realize that that was the nature of his offence at the time, and I interceded for him and secured a position for him in the government telegraph service in western Canada. He had been in contact with those people in the vicinity of Edmonton who were I believe responsible for this whole trouble which developed in South Oxford. It was directed by those people, and he was the manipulator in getting the names improperly placed on the voters' list. I intimated that I would have those men arrested. I started out determined to do so, and I did not understand until later, when I went to the registrar, that this young man had made an affidavit that those people were entitled to vote, although he knew very well, that they had only been in the township a few days. They were living on a car on the Canadian National Railways, and I believe were brought into the constituency to vote against me. One of them, the foreman, when subpoenaed'-and they were only served with subpoenaes after they had got out of the constituency and were on their way east-admitted in court that their names were on the voters' list in the province of Qudbec, and they were anxious to go back there because they had just learned that they had not been in South Oxford long
Adjournment-Customs Inquiry

enough to entitle them to vote. The news spread quickly that I was going to have them arrested, and they were already on their way east when served with summonses to appear; it was only by means of a swift automobile that we were able to overtake them and 'have them brought back. Does the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) think that the statement made by him in the House yesterday that bootleggers had been employed against him by the Tory party and were being backed up by them is going to receive much credence?
The government are responsible 4 p.m. for bootleggers. Do not forget that. They cannot shift the responsibility to any other quarter. It is admitted that smuggling on a very large scale has been going on, and the government have been charged by an hon. member of this House with a guilty knowledge of the illicit traffic, so they cannot shift their responsibility to any other quarter. The fact that parliament last session voted 8350,000, and that only 823,100 has been spent in an attempt to cope with the evil, is sufficient to condemn them. There is not any question as to that.
Now, Mr. Speaker, before leaving the election scandal in South Oxford, I am going to refer just for a moment to a letter which I sent to the chief electoral officer, because I do not know whether or not it will appear in his report:
Ingersoll, December 24, 1925.
Colonel O. M. Bjggar,
Chief Electoral Officer,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,
I have vour letter of the 11th inst., regarding complaints made by me against certain election officers in South Oxford.
In view of your correspondence with returning officer C. H. Denton on the matter, I cannot agree with your suggestion. for elaborating and defining more clearly the appellation which I employed, and which, Sir, I should like to draw to the attention of the Minister of Customs and Excise was not applied to members of parliament generally but only to those on his own side of the House. The member for Labelle described them as voters for the principles and policies enunciated by that newly constituted committee of parliament-himself, the member for Brandon and the member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Since the recent igeneral election things have changed very materially in the Dominion. During the campaign the Prime Minister announced to the country that there were four great issues before the electors-transportation, immigration, fiscal policy and Senate reform. Since the newly constituted committee of parliament has taken office we find these are no longer the great national issues. We find the member for Brandon dictating to this House that instead of considering the transportation problem, we are to vote money to build the Hudson Bay railway; we find the member for Winnipeg North Centre saying that instead of having an immigration policy or attempting to find work for our unemployed, we shall have a policy of doles; we find the member for Brandon also saying that instead of considering any fiscal policy we shall devote our attention to rural credits; and again we find the member for Winnipeg North Centre-realizing I suppose that by his conduct in this House he has lost the confidence *f his electors and "will not much longer retain his seat-we find him dictating to the

Prime Minister that Senate reform shall be abandoned and instead thereof that we shall consider a policy of old age pensions. Thus is he making sure of his own future.
Now, Sir, possibly the absence of the member for Brandon is accounted for by the fact that, realizing there is not going to be an adjournment until March 15 in which to 5 pan. prepare his legislation, he is now occupying his time in preparing a measure for rural credits. I think the silence of the Minister of Justice on Tuesday is amply accounted for by the fact that he had no valid reason to give for the proposed adjournment, and that the member for Brandon when he rose to attempt to justify the proposal lost his nerve; he could not face the House and give the real reason. Whether it was fear of an investigation into the charges made by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre or whether the proposal was put forward to enable the Progressive leader to prepare his legislation, I want to point out to the hon. gentleman and to his supporters the seriousness of the situation now confronting the House and the country. During the past, few weeks we have had in this House the clearest confession of impotency, the most unequivocal1 and pitiable confession that this government is incapable of submitting to parliament one piece of constructive legislation for the good of the country; in a word, the gentlemen now occupying the treasury benches have confessed that they cannot carry on as a government. We have had presented to parliament charges of the %most serious nature, the like of which has not been know in our parliamentary history. Yet in the face of all that this government asks my friends the Progressives to vote for delay, to vote time for two or three of its supporters to seek seats in this House. I suggest to the members of the Progressive party that the country will not tolerate an adjournment of this House, it will not tolerate any tampering with the interests of the Dominion at this critical juncture. This situation is fraught with serious consequences, and I suggest to my hon. friends of the Progressive party that they will be sounding their own death knell and that of their party should they align themselves with a government which attempts to delay the investigation of charges as serious as those now before this House. I warn them that the call sounded by this government to-day is the last desperate call for help from tMr. J. A. Clark.]

Mr. JEAN J. DENIS (Jol'iette):	Mr. Speaker, I am afraid this debate has degenerated into mere stump speeches and political propaganda. On the one hand we have the opposition saying, 'We want to do business; get to business," and on the other we have here anything but business. I have listened to the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland); he was out of order all the time, and hon. members know it well. I rose to a point of order and Mr. Speaker gave the hon. member the benefit of the doubt. That was a good ruling, but we know the hon. gentleman was, strictly speaking, out of order. The hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) was also out of order most of the time.
What is the question before the House? 1 will try to confine myself strictly to that question in my remarks. The question is, whether this House should adjourn for a certain period of time, as indicated in the motion and is the amendment to that motion sufficient to prevent this House from granting that adjournment? That is the question. We will examine first of all the motion to adjourn, and then the merits of the amendment. The amendment says:
This House having been called in session at the instance of the present government, and a number of legislative and other proposals submitted for its consideration by said government in the form of a Speech from the Throne, it is the duty of the House, should the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne be adopted, to proceed with the public business until same is disposed of.
Now, Sir, can you imagine anything more contrary to logic than the position taken by the opposition? They have been saying for one month that this government does not exist. They have used every adjective in the English language against the government, and now they claim that after the Speech from the Throne is voted-if it is voted by the House-the government has all power and should proceed with the business of parliament. And not only do they say they should proceed, but that it is the duty of the government to proceed with business and that they have no right to ask for adjournment. I say that not only has the government the right to ask for an adjournment, but that right has already been recognized by parliament. Much more will it be recognized when the vote on the Address is taken, if this vote is favourable.
What have we had? In the first instance we had a government convening parliament and asking whether or not this government should carry on the affairs of the country.

Adjournment-Customs Inquiry
What, was the result of that question? Parliament, the supreme master of the situation, answered yes; answered that the government should have convened parliament, should have remained in office and should have submitted their case to the House. That being so, the government presented to parliament the Speech from the Throne and asked that it be discussed. Then what occurred? The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) proposed an amendment to the Speech from the Throne which, if carried would have defeated the Speech, having the same effect as a morion of non-confidence. What was the result? A vote was taken on that amendment and again parliament declared that the government-should 'carry on, that it should remain in office, notwithstanding the fact that our friends on the other side rise one after another and call upon the government to resign, as against the wish expressed by parliament itself. But we have more than that. This motion to adjourn will only take effect if and when the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne is voted by parliament. What will it mean? If the Address is voted by parliament it will mean that the House, by the third vote within a month, will be calling upon this government to carry on and conduct the affairs of the country. Then, the government having received a mandate from parliament on three different occasions within a month, will anyone say that it is not justified in carrying on? Not only is it justified in so doing, but it is its duty to carry on. What is the situation? When the first vote was taken, this House by a majority of three declared that the government should remain in office. When the second vote was taken there was a majority of ten, again expressing the wishes of the House. When a third vote is taken and a third majority given-because we expect it to come out that way, or otherwise the motion has no object -the House will have declared for the third time that the government must remain in office. Then it is for the government to organize and carry on the affairs of the country. I say that when the first vote was taken this government received an implicit right to organize its cabinet and fill in the gaps. Surely it is no argument to come befoie parliament and say to the government "You have lost nine ministers, and therefore you cannot cany on." Parliament is seized with the situation and parliament must decide as to whether or not this government, which has gone to the country and been returned as it has been returned, should continue in office

Oh, oh.

Assuming this to
be true

and it is not right, it is not proper, it is supremely unjust to the government to use such expressions-what have we got? Oh, oh.

opposite may laugh but that is the consequence, it is the inevitable consequence, of the judgment of parliament. There is nothing to laugh at.

May not the position of the hon. member for Labelle be this, that he thinks he can do more with a crippled party than with a robust one?

The distinction is a little fine so I will permit the hon. gentleman to find an answer himself. Moreover, I am not the spokesman for the hon. member for Labelle. I say that the amendment of the hon. member (Mr. Stevens) is first of all an admission that this government will be able to carry on, should carry on, and will have the duty of carrying on immediately the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne has been adopted. This is perfectly clear, but with the task of carrying on is associated the duty of reorganizing. This duty of reorganizing has existed ever since parliament was convened.

May I ask the hon.
member a question?

I would prefer that the hon. gentleman would not do so until I have finished my sentence. As I was about to say, the task of reorganizing existed immediately after the election. Would the government have acted as they have done had they been so anxious to remain in power as hon. gentlemen have alleged so many times? Had the government wanted to retain office, irrespective of the opinion of parliament, they

could have reorganized and come back. But that would not alter the situation. They would be the same government with the same number of members behind them, namely about one hundred. They would not be any stronger, and by so doing they would have undertaken themselves to render judgment, whereas that responsibility devolved upon parliament. Now that judgment has been rendered, now that parliament has declared that the government must carry on, there is an implied command, an obligation on their part, to reorganize, take the time necessary to do so, return to parliament, and continue to administer public affairs as long as they receive the support of parliament.

If, as the hon. member has stated, parliament has declared its perfect satisfaction with this government, and its perfect confidence in the ability of the government to carry on, why is it asked to abdicate its functions and go back home for six weeks?
There has been no abdication by parliament.

When this judgment was rendered by parliament the conditions were known by parliament. All those members who voted for the government knew that the government could not carry on without going again to the country and having certain of their ministers elected.

May I ask one more
question? Has any member of the government stated to parliament that they could not carry on, or that they were unable to function as a government?

I would answer
my hon. friend in this way: Is it in the interest of the country that the government should be represented here only by one-half or two-thirds of the ministers? Rather is it in the interest of the country that the government should carry on as it is going to do, as parliament rightly or wrongly has decided it should do, and it must in order to organize have its ministers elected. This cannot be done during a session of parliament.
It will be said that this is something extraordinary, something which has never happened before. But parliament has been adjourned before. Let us suppose however that the situation is an exceptional one, and that parliament has never before adjourned in order to secure the election of ministers,, is it not also true that never in the history of this country has there been a situation such as exists to-day? It is an exceptional situation

which has to be met by exceptional means, and parliament has decided that it should be so. Surely parliament has not decided that the government should be carried on by two-thirds of the ministry. Parliament having decided what the proper course should be the government is now seeking to give effect to that decision.
So much for the first part of the amendment. In the second part of the amendment it is stated that the adjournment cannot be granted because there is to be an inquiry into the Customs department. That is the trouble. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) in a great speech tries to demonstrate to this House how perfectly unjust it would be to leave this matter in abeyance for six weeks when it should be dealt with immediately. He says that the committee must be appointed at once, and that no adjournment shall take place until the committee is appointed, and the investigation proceeded with. What is the answer of the government? The government answers, through the Minister of Customs, "Not only will we grant you this inquiry, but we will go much further than you ask us to go and give you the most complete investigation; the committee will proceed, not to deal with a period of two years but with a period of twenty years if you like." That is the declaration of the Minister of Customs, and he invites the opposition to co-operate with him and investigate. Having received no answer, he rose again on Wednesday and asked to be permitted to make a declaration to the House. He said: "I declare to the House once more that I am ready, and the government is ready, to appoint that committee". What is the opposition doing? Instead of consenting to the appointment of the committee they continue to make speeches. I have no objection to that, but it is absolutely out of order, because what is sought by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre is not a verdict against the government at this stage. Surely his speech was not delivered with the object of having a debate on it? Yet we are having that debate. Is such a course logical, is it practical or is it just? Whyi are we having this debate? For political propaganda, and for that purpose only. The procedure is well known. The hon. member makes a charge and asks that a committee be appointed and the government answers and says, "We agree and we will make it even better than you have asked for". With all due consideration and respect, what business have members on the other side of the House to rise in their places and bring charge
after charge against the government, precisely on this great issue upon which the opposition is asking that a committee be appointed to enquire into the conditions of the Customs department?

Does the hon. member not think it is highly important in the public interest that that committee should get to work at once and that there should be no recess or adjournment for six weeks in the interim?
What is to prevent them sitting?
The Minister of Customs on two successive days stated in this House, "I am ready, let us appoint a committee". What more do you want?
Does the hon. member not know that negotiations are proceeding between the Minister of Customs and the leader of the opposition as to the appointment of that committee?

I am very glad to hear that. It makes the position of my hon. friends very much worse. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) is a clever lawyer and will understand it. While negotiations are under way they want a tribunal appointed. This committee will be a tribunal to try the case and hon. members on the other side of the House are guilty of the impropriety of rendering judgment before the case has been submitted to the tribunal. That is exactly the situation.

Does the hon. member not understand that all these considerations he is mentioning would constitute an objection to the adjournment of the House and an argument for proceeding at once with the investigation of the charges?

Not by any means, and I will tell the hon. member why. The committee can be appointed, and with the consent of the House can function during the adjournment. I have too much respect for the knowledge of my hon. friend to think that he does not know that. He knows it perfectly well. The committee can be appointed, and with the consent of the House they can sit all through the adjournment until we meet again. Therefore it is not correct to say that if we adjourn the House the committee cannot function. The statement of the Minister of Customs was "This committee will have the right to hear witnesses, send for papers and documents, to move from place to place," and so on. It

will have very wide powers and it can exercise those powers during the adjournment. Is that a reason why we should not adjourn?
Coming back to the other point, I say that the opposition is guilty of a great impropriety in calling for a tribunal, which tribunal must decide the case, and before that tribunal is appointed, rising in this House and continuing the attack against the government in the same way as might be done if the committee had heard the evidence and reported. There will be a proper time for the attacks, if there are to be any attacks, and a time for the government to defend themselves, and that time will be after the committee has reported to this! House. The committee will inquire into the charges, make a report to this House, and on the motion to adopt or reject the report every member of this House will have the right to make a speech, and that will be the opportune time to discuss the question. Whatever is being said in the meantime is political propaganda.
The hon. member has Stated that the committee is to function during the recess of parliament.
If parliament adjourns.

If the House adjourns and the committee holds its sessions, the members of parliament are scattered all over the country. Suppose the committee in its investigation, within one week or ten days or so after it has begun to function, discovers something that parliament should immediately deal with, what are we going to do?
That will not occur.
Pure imagination.

The committee will be appointed to deal with this question and the committee functions outside of parliament and independent of parliament until it reports to parliament.
I have abstained from giving advice to my colleagues and I am not going to advise them now, but if we want to discuss questions frankly, honestly and intelligently, let us follow those rules which were enacted long, long ago-those rules which have given justice at all times and in all parliaments to both the plaintiff and the defendant, to both the government and the opposition. Let us proceed regularly. Let us have this committee appointed. Let us have this committee function. Let U3 have this committee report to parliament, and when the time comes after the

report has been made, let us discuss that report of the committee. So much for the amendment. If we leave that aside, if we take into consideration the fact that what is Sought in the amendment was granted immediately by the government, I ask: Is there any purpose in that amendment except to block the business of this House? I am afraid unfortunately that is what is going on now. Therefore, my humble opinion is that if hon. members on the other side of the House are serious, sincere, they should accept the proposition of the government to appoint a committee, let the committee function, and follow the wish of parliament by letting the government organize. Then we shall come back to parliament and dispose of these matters.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to address to the House some remarks which, I hope, will be very brief upon this amendment. One would hardly have the hardihood to do so after what has fallen from the lips of the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis), if it were not for the fact, as he, or, at leapt, his leaders must know, that the terms of this investigation are now under consideration, and if decided or completed, I do not think I would very long occupy the time of the House. I hope I shall not repeat what has already been said in this debate. I am unalterably opposed to a six weeks' holiday. I adopt all the arguments that have been advanced on this side, and I say frankly that I cannot conceive any reason that concerns this country, why this House should take a holiday.
I wish to make some remarks concerning the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) and his speech on Tuesday last. I frankly admire the minister. I think the strategy of his deliverance on the non-confidence motion, saved the Liberal party from defeat. I was asked by a Quebec member what I thought of his speech on Tuesday night. I said that I thought it was the best apology that could be made in the circumstances, and I believe so still. The minister is a learned counsel, and I have no doubt he has often given the advice to men who have sought it, that when they are caught with the goods, they should make a clean breast of it. So, we find that when the minister was caught with the goods, he pulled out of his pocket a resolution which he had prepared dealing with the whole question, and in order to make a cleaner breast of it, he tells us that he is going to offer us something which is wider and better than was asked for in our own resolution. I congratulate the minister on being so beforehand with the work of his department. He told us this afternoon that

Adjournment-Customs Inquiry
he was slow to get started, but he is certainly one of those "stretch" runners, so that when it comes to the last lap, he can make up a great deal of time. He expected and, no doubt, still expects that this adjournment will be approved by the House. We find that although he did not, upon his own confession, undertake the responsibility and work attached to a minister in his department when he was appointed, yet, as he tells us this afternoon, a long time ago he prepared the resolution which he offered us on Tuesday. I want to question the frankness of this offer. We find, when we propose a remedy for the situation, that the minister has all ready, cut and dried, and prepared, a resolution. Would it not have been proper, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) suggested, that the government, realizing the necessity for this investigation, should have acted immediately this parliament assembled? Could this not have been put in the Speech from the Throne? The minister admits that frauds have been committed on the customs and that criminal infractions of the law have taken place. So does the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). So does the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), who says that he knew what was going on, and if it matters, so does the Prime Minister. We have one member of the government who says that our desire for an investigation is a mere bluff. Not only was that said once, but it was referred to the second time. We have this situation, that the resolution which has been proposed by the minister was not given to the House until it was dragged from him, and, therefore, I question its good faith. Within my experience I knew of a confidential clerk who was embezzling money and whose plan was to take a sum of money out of the vault and then to write out his cheque for the amount with some little interest added. One hundred dollars would be taken and a cheque for $105 put in his pocket, so that if there was detection, he could say: "Oh, I only borrowed this money. Here is a cheque with interest for the amount that I have taken." When we are actually imperilled in this country over customs frauds and we desire that the government or so-called government should act, and when we raise the question, we are told by the minister that he has had the matter under consideration for a long time and here is a resolution that he proposes to move when the matter comes up. Do hon. members think the country will be satisfied with the bona tides of the government in pressing an investigation of these very frauds which they knew of for months and months? I submit not.
The situation may be tested in another way. We have urged: Why was this duty not undertaken by the government sooner? Then, comes the opposite: Why this delay? The motion for the six weeks' adjournment came after the resolution calling for this investigation into customs frauds had been placed on the order paper, but they were willing to delay the investigation for at least six weeks longer, because it could not have been dealt with until the House reassembled after the proposed holiday. There is another evidence of the unwillingness of the government and its dilatoriness to act in this matter when we consider the attitude of the minister. Many a murderer before he has been hanged has expressed as his last wish: "Let me know who was it that squealed on me?" After the bars have clanged behind many a prisoner, his chief ' desire in life is to know who squealed on him. And we find the minister rising in his place and telling the House how anxious he is for an investigation and giving us a committee of nine members instead of seven. There is the interest on the cheque, and then he says to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, "But who did tell you? Was it Mr. A. or Mr. B.? Did you arrive at Montreal with Mr. C, or was it from Mr. D that you got. the information?" Why was the minister so very keen to ascertain the source of the information received by our party when he avers that he is so very anxious to carry out a proper investigation? The minister referred to the Duncan report; and what does he tell us about it? How keen the man must have been, who had the attitude of the minister towards the Duncan report, to hold an inquiry because, as he says, he desires a clean administration. The Duncan report was put in his pocket, where the resolution came from, and then he felt it was not safe in his pocket and he put it in a safe, as he tells us, with a combination lock on it. And then he is deeply concerned to know, did Duncan tell anything that led you to ask for the inquiry? Is that the attitude of a minister of the government who wants a fair, honest, thorough-paced inquiry into these gross custom frauds?
The minister also declared to us what his policy was with his department. He said, "When an official is accused I suspend; when he is found guilty I dismiss; when he is found not guilty I restore." Loud cheers from those sitting around him. Mr. Speaker, I submit that this minister who desires a clean administration had some other duty to perform. When guilt is established, not only should dismissal follow, but if the official has transgressed the laws of this land, if he has brought himself subject to an information,

it is the minister's duty to see that that information is laid; and when he suspends an official who, he has reason and probable cause to believe, has been a criminal against the laws of this country it is his duty not to stop at suspension but to put that criminal in a place where he is safe against his trial and where he cannot make away with the evidence against him. Did the minister do that in the case of Bisaillon? He says he read the report and that the charges against the man were grave and serious; he uses both words. Then what does he do? He puts the report in the safe, where it was until the time he spoke on Tuesday. He takes no action against Bisaillon, although the occasion for action was so grave that, as he says, he immediately dictated the memorandum for council to net upon. And when he finds out that this report was so grave, which demanded instant action, part of which he took, he leaves the report in the safe. He is concerned over it, but no action whatever is taken against Bisaillon except dismissal, nor is any action taken against anyone who may be involved in that report.
I submit that it was the duty of the Minister of Customs to have an information laid immediately against Bisaillon if he knew of any infraction by him of the criminal law. That report, as the minister avers, he has read, and I venture to think-I know nothing, I am only surmising-that it involves others. And if that report involves others who have transgressed the law of this land and the Minister of Customs has taken no action against either Bisaillon or other parties referred to therein, >1 want to tell the minister, as I tell the House, that this country will hold him personally responsible, because he has connived at criminals against the law of Canada and allowed them to go unwhipped of justice. I submit that we as members of parliament have a right to see this Duncan report; I submit that it should be laid on the table of the House. Oh, but someone may say that if you lay a report of that kind on the table the criminals will get away. Does anyone mean to tell me that after what has taken place in the House these criminals have not already got on the move and that the evidence Which would convict them is not being spirited away? I say that no harm but only benefit can result from that report being laid on the table of the House and the criminal law being put in motion against those who have offended. Why has the minister delayed thus long? The government will never end these terrific assaults on our customs until action is taken against the perpetrators, and I am sure it is the wish of the 
House that every measure be taken by the government to bring these criminals to justice. tNo excuse will be listened to. There is no use saying that someone is involved, it does not matter whether he 'be Tory or Liberal; the law of the land is committed to the charge of the ministers and if they fail in their duty the people will hold them to account.

At six o'dock, Mr. Speaker, I was referring to the Duncan report, the minister's treatment of Bisaillon, and his treatment of the report itself. That report, the minister says, should have been known to no one but Duncan who made it and to himself who received it, and that the import of it was so great that he took immediate action. He says that he is not a friend of Bisaillon, that that man's interests are .not the minister's. One would gather from what he says so emphatically that if any action was to be taken against Bisaillon the minister was quite prepared to take it. The question naturally arises:	If frauds have 'been committed, why was action not taken? If the minister the very day that lhe received the report communicated its essentials to council, and council dismissed Bisaillon, then there must have been in that report convincing evidence of a crime by Bisaillon against the country.
Were others involved? Naturally the inference is that they were. If not, why the

Adjournment-Customs Inquiry
secrecy with regard to the report? Why could it not have been, kept even in the pocket of the minister, why did it have to be put in a safe under a combination lock? I serve notice now on the minister-and I regret that he is not in his seat-that if the report contains evidence of offences committed against the country by Bisaillon or others, and the Minister of Customs and Excise and the Minister of Justice, whose duty it was, failed to take action, then they and the government will be held responsible in public opinion.
And why delay? Is there any other reason than that it is well known that the best advocate any defendant can possibly have is delay? This is an old adage familiar to every lawyer. Hon. gentlemen laugh. Well, I suppose that if this suggestion were adopted it would be a violation of some precedent, one of those sacred traditions that we must not touch. But really 1 think .we attach too much importance in this House to precedents. We are always talking about what happened some time in the past, and I sometimes think that if our ancestors had always based religiously upon principle, everything they did, they might still be moving around in the water like wigglors-because I accept the evolution theory. I imagine that one of the first three dwellers who introduced the innovation of moving along the ground may have been driven out of his community When he assumed an upright position, for 1 presume that he was regarded as a radical! who was breaking some precedent. We should not be too much afraid of that sort of thing. . As a (matter of fact we are continually breaking precedents, and ll see no reason why the suggestion I have just offered should not be accepted by hon. gentlemen to my right. I assume that the government has no other reason for asking for an adjournment than to ibe enabled to hold the byelections, and if they and the official opposition could agree to what I have proposed we could go on with the business of the House. There is not much that they can agree on, but in the event of their being unable to make such an arrangement they might give to the .members of this group full information as to what their programme is to be.

I think perhaps the hon. gentleman's suggestion might more readily be adopted if he put it the other- way. Instead of the opposition pairing with 'the government, how would it do for the government to pair with the Progressives? Has the hon. gentleman any objection to that proposal?

I fail! to see any force in the suggestion. The Progressives are being accused of supporting the government all the time and there would be no advantage in pairs between government and Progressive members. However, if the government is not able to make some arrangement with the official opposition, they might lay before the members of this group their legislative programme for the six weeks-assuming that they are supported on the Address and are
installed in office-and some gentleman s agreement might be arrived at whereby the business of the House could be (carried on, and they could go ahead with their by-elections. Notwithstanding the laughter with which some hon. gentlemen greet my suggestion, I hope that they will consider it. I know that they are all active business men who have many things to attend to at home and it would foe better for all of us and for the country generally if we (could proceed with the sessional programme. If we did that we should cease to make ourselves ridiculous in the eyes of the people by holding up the business of the country. In this regard I am speaking collectively, because I take a share of the responsibility to myself. And 1 say that we (are .making ourselves ridiculous. Can we not adopt some such suggestion as I have made and allow the government to go on with the by-elections and simultaneously proceed with the business of the House?

As I
have sat here for a month now, with a patience that has not manifested itself in other quarters, I hope I shall be pardoned for saying a few words even if they do not add very much to the discussion. As member after member has taken the opportunity in his opening remarks to extend to you, Mr. Speaker, felicitations on your re-election to the high office you occupy, it has occurred to me that the custom is a graceful one, but I have since learned to appreciate the fact that the congratulations offered were both personal and sincere. I have come to this conclusion not only from observing the patient dignity with which you discharge the duties of your office but from the kindly consideration you show to younger members of the House when they transgress or threaten to transgress the rules of the House, and the gentle firmness with which you lead them back to the path of propriety. May I also say that I am sure the younger men all' appreciate the kindly reception given them by the older members on the occasion of their maiden speeches.
But although I have been impressed with the foregoing, as well as in other ways, I hope it will not be considered presumptuous of me to observe that I have not been impressed with what this House has accomplished. After the protestations of all parties to the electorate, the emphatic declarations as to policy, the promises of performance and the resounding demands for vigour in administration and for a courageous grappling, with the problems of this country, I should have thought that the people would have a right

to expect that when the members of this House assembled they would proceed with despatch to implement their undertakings. But the proverbial mouse brought forth by the mountain assumes heroic proportions in comparison with what we have accomplished.
We have in this House a large number of new members and I think I may safely assume that they at least embody the protest on the part of this country against the vacillation, the inactivity and the failure to deal with the pressing problems of Canada which have characterised the government of the last three or four years. There is not the slightest doubt that the country is faced with grave problems, and candidate after candidate, every member in this House I believe, took the platform some time ago and assured the people that if elected they would see to it that there would be a vigorous performance in this House of the promises they then made. If, therefore, we agree to this adjournment, in the absence of any accomplishment whatever, I say that we are making ourselves accessories to a continuation of existing conditions. Even if we had not had1 the disclosure of the grave charges which have been made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), I would still say that we had too many things of importance to attend to to think of adjourning. But the charges made by that hon. member are so grave and serious, charges in the making of which he is taking his political life in his hands if he cannot substantiate them, that I do not think this House should consider for a moment any proposal to adjourn. I do not think that there is a single member here who does not believe that those charges are correct in toto.
But what of the other problems? You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister of this country stated to the people that there were pressing and important problems which demanded immediate solution, and those on this side of the House took the same view and outlined the policy which in their opinion should be adopted to solve those problems. Now the House is assembled and the government is undertaking to carry on, presumably for the purpose of putting into effect the things which they assured the people were necessary for the future prosperity of Canada. When the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) made his want of confidence motion a good many members of the Progressive party intimated their disapproval of that motion because there was something in the Speech from the Throne which, according to the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) , had certain attractions. I have listened

to addresses in this House from government and from Progressive benches; I have read the Speech from the Throne carefully and tried to analyze it; and I have read those speeches which I did not hear in person. I have failed completely to discover any single reason why the Progressives should be enamoured of even those things they say the government has promised. I have seldom seen a document so evasive in its terms, a document that promised so little and yet may be said to promise so much; that can be construed in one way in one section of the country and in another way in other sections. I hope I may have the indulgence of the House while I go very briefly through this wonderful Speech from the Throne.
The first clause is a boast by the government of the wonderful prosperity that Canada is enjoying. Now, I have faith in the Dominion. I believe that not even a succession of inefficient governments can in any way permanently hamper the advancement of the country. But I say to the gentlemen who occupy the benches opposite, that for them to make the time-honoured boast that every government makes and to claim credit for national prosperity is to be guilty of the most biting irony.
They boast of the growth in our exports. Where is that growth? In agricultural products and wood pulp. Is any policy of the government responsible for that increase? There is one item in the list of exports that I think they can claim credit for-six million and a half dollars of settlers' effects. Those were the effects of our young men, leaving Canada perhaps forever. I should like to know what profit the Dominion received from that exodus. Then they speak of the growth in our imports. An analysis of the substantial items of our imports will show how ridiculous is the claim that the government is responsible for the prosperity of the country. For instance, we imported
155.000.	000 worth of coal. Already this
session we have heard of the deplorable condition of the coal miners of Nova Scotia. We could produce every single pound of the coal we imported.	Another big item is
8140.000.	000 worth of steel and steel products -the direct result of the tariff changes made by the government opposite. We have in Selkirk, the leading town in the constituency that I represent, a steel foundry and a rolling mill. I know from personal experience the detrimental effect upon the business of those two plants from the changes made in the tariff by the government last session or the session before. An hon. member on the
