opposite side remarked during the course of
the debate that the debit balance against Canada in our trade relations with the United States was growing less. It is still between $100,000,000 and $200,000,000. What consolation can the government derive from that state of affairs? Surely it is not because the Progressives believe that this government is responsible for any growth in prosperity that they desire to continue it in office?
Now I come to immigration. Although I heard a great many speeches delivered by Progressive candidates during the recent election, I have not heard that the Progressive party as a whole is ardently in favour of an active immigration policy, nor have I heard any very strong approval from the Labour group. This is a subject that I am keenly interested in, and I hope at some future time to have an opportunity to add something to the knowledge of the House respecting immigration. This, however, I wish to say now, that although I am in favour of a vigorous immigration policy, I think the first duty of the government is to have a policy that will keep at home our native born Canadians. There is no use bringing in settlers and putting them on the land without making adequate provision to enable them to remain there. In my constituency we have two lines of railway. Twenty years ago settlers were placed along those lines by the Dominion government. I refer to the Ruthenians. They have been augmented in number by some soldier settlers-also placed there by the federal government. You know, Sir, the province of Manitoba has not control of its natural resources. The title to all land, occupied or unoccupied is vested in the Dominion. Under such conditions it is impossible to finance those districts, to provide roads, and other facilities. Any provincial organization is practically impossible, and yet the government of Canada has been putting men on those lands, but has utterly failed to make any provision for the necessary services which would enable the settlers to derive any benefit from their work. Hundreds of families have left the district because they were flooded out or could not market their crops. A few days ago I received letters from three settlers asking that I obtain from the Department of Immigration assistance in moving their effects from their farms that they can neither use nor sell. Any policy of immigration that does not give settlers a proper start in life is a failure. A policy of vigorous immigration cannot appeal to our Progressive friends.
We believe in the policy the hon. member has outlined, a policy that will keep the people who are here on the land, rather than bring more people in to take the place of settlers who have moved out.

I am quite aware that some members of the Progressive party have advocated a policy that will keep the people at home, but others have expressed themselves strongly against any policy of immigration at all. I believe the members of the party from Alberta are strongly of opinion that we should not inaugurate a vigorous policy of immigration.
The Hudson Bay railway is another matter that I am greatly interested in, and I hope I shall have the opportunity of discussing it later in the session. The Speech from the Throne contains a promise for "completion forthwith" of this railway. For what purpose? There is no question that the Hudson Bay railway as originally demanded by the west was to convey to tidewater the cattle and grain of the west and develop that northern country. Northern Manitoba has as much potential wealth as northern Ontario. We have there a wooded area as extensive as that of Sweden, and of much the same kmd. Sweden realizes for her people $100,000,000 annually; we realize less than a million dollars. There is a rich development possible in the fisheries both in the bay and in the rivers. The railway is necessary for that development. At the present time it seems to me that the real purpose of the Hudson Bay railway undertaking is to convey back to Ottawa the Prime Minister of this country. I want to say to our Progressive friends that there are as many sincere supporters of the completion of the Hudson Bay railway in this quarter as will be found in any other section of the House. But we favour real construction, construction that will mean something to the west; not a comparatively small grant of a million or less that will enable only a very inadequate amount of work to be undertaken. We will fight for the completion of the Hudson -Bay railway. I am sure that the Progressives know that they have stout friends of the Hudson Bay railway in this quarter; there is no western Conservative member who is not in favour of it. Our leader has promised that when means shall be found he will complete the road; and our Progressive friends know that a promise of the right hon. leader of the opposition means something.

The next matter dealt with in this wonderful Speech from the Throne is rural credits. The right hon. leader of the opposition has said that he is in favour of a sensible scheme of rural credits. We have had an unfortunate experience in Manitoba with rural credits. WTe do not want any rural credit scheme that will mean further loss to the province as1 well as to the Dominion. Any scheme should be based, as the right hon. leader of the opposition has said, upon the land bank system and an intermediate credit board. The government has neither expounded nor explained what it intends to do in this regard, but I am sure our Progressive friends know that if the rural credit scheme is upon a sound business basis it will receive unanimous support from this side of the House. It is not and cannot be that that is what makes' them feel that this programme is so attractive.
Then we come to that subject which has been so much discussed, the tariff. I may say at the outset that I am a convinced and confirmed protectionist. In my constituency are all kinds of people; it is a cross-section of Canada, with labouring people, market gardeners, mill-workers, fishermen, farmers, dairymen, lumbermen all there. From one end of that constituency to the other I talked protection, and I think I voiced the views of Manitoba on the question of protection. There is not the slightest doubt in my mind that Manitoba favours protection; there is no doubt that the Labour members of this parliament know that their constituents favour protection also, I have read the clause in the Speech from the Throne touching on that subject, and from the remarks of Progressives which I have heard I do not think they have considered or read the clause as it is found in that Speech. May I take up the time of the House for a few minutes to read the salient part of that clause:
They believe that in the interest of industrial development every effort should be made to eliminate the element of uncertainty with respect to tariff changes; that changes in the tariff should be made only after the fullest examination of their bearing upon both primary and manufacturing industries and that representations requesting increase or decrease of duties should be made the subject of the most careful investigation and report by a body possessing the necessary qualifications to advise the Ministry with respect thereto.
In the light of the declarations made by
the Prime Minister at Richmond Hill, what comfort can any free trader-if there is any such animal-now take from this clause in the Speech? If it is not a direct confession that the Liberal party is now converted to the policy of protection, I do not know what it is.

May I say to my hon.
friend that as a Progressive I am not under any delusions in that respect. Those of us who have been in this House for four years recognize the fact that the two national parties are both protectionist.

I am very glad to
receive that assurance, because I am sure the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) in his own heart knows that protection is the definite and settled policy of Canada. There never will be a departure from that principle, no matter what party is in power. Although an agitation against it went on for many years, Canada will not depart from that principle, which was essential to the making of this nation of ours. When Canada became a confederated dominion the principle of protection was not then adopted, but it became the policy in 1878, and since that time although there have been departures from it that policy has remained, and it was settled in this last election if it had not been settled before.
I have tried to analyse the principal statements in that Speech from the Throne, and I ask the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) which clause is so alluring that he wants to maintain in power a government which has lost the confidence of the country, *which does not possess the confidence of this House and which has not the ability to function.

May I say to my hon.
friend that if the government had depended on my vote it would not have been in power to-day. In answer to his direct question I would say that the attractive items of legislation outlined in the Speech from the Throne are those referring to the Hudson Bay railway and rural credits. I am not interested in the other niceties about the weather, the prosperity of the country and so on.

I am satisfied that
the hon. member for Mackenzie will, when he comes to consider his vote, remember that the Hudson Bay railway has been dangled before the eyes of the Progressives before and that also applies to the rural credits measure. I am sure the hon. member has confidence in the leader of the opposition, and when he has heard assertions such as my right hon. leader has made on the floor of this House, I think he will be satisfied that those promises contained in the Speech from the Throne alone are not a justification for maintaining this government in office.
.Now I want to go briefly over the policy of protection as I understand it. The charge

has been widely made that the Conservative party is a high tariff party. I am sure hon. members of this House know that the right hon. leader of the opposition is quite capable of expressing himself with such clarity that there can be no mistaking his views. He moved in this House a resolution, which speaks for itself, and in it there is no word of high tariff. He promises that his party will carry out the principle of protection, that that will be the basis on which it will work, but the height of that tariff is a matter for the experts to determine, so long as they recognize the principle that all industries, including agriculture must be safeguarded. I want also to say that although there is a vague reference to the farming community in this tariff provision in the Speech from the Throne, it means little. I remember that the Liberal candidate for South Winnipeg, a gentleman who had the confidence of the leader of this government as few men had; a gentleman who was going to be one of his mainstays in this House, published in the papers in Winnipeg a statement something like this:	"If
Meighen is elected your food will cost you more." There never was any intention on the part of that man, who has always been considered friendly to the Progressives, to stand for a low tariff policy, yet there never was any intention on his part to give protection to the farmers of this country. The Conservative party1 has promised protection to the dairying industry, the fruit growers, the cattle men, the poultry men, and all those who produce in Canada. They will be considered when the tariff is framed.
Now I am asking my Progressive friends whether they have really considered what is happening in the west to-day. Last September and October potatoes were selling for twenty-five, thirty and forty cents a bushel, which was below the cost of production. Why? Because potatoes had come in earlier from the United States; the market was gone;
transportation costs were too high to allow them to ship to the markets of the east, and the market to the south was barred to them by the tariff. To provide for that and for the grain growers as well, the right hon. leader of the opposition promised to assist the transportation of the primary products of this country from the west to the consuming centres of the east. Progressive members must know that that problem can only be met by direct subvention by this parliament. With the railway losses we have sustained, it is a direct promise that while helping these industries of the west this party will, by subvention, give them relief. Is there any
Progressive member from the west who does not want to have lower transportation costs? Does any hon. member believe that result can be obtained without losses which will have to be borne by the country as a whole? If they are in favour of that plan, why should they not favour the subvention by tariff, if I may so call it? How can they be in favour of one system and not of the other?
The last speaker made a suggestion which caused some members amusement. I considered it to be an earnest effort to help himself escape and aid his brother Progressives to escape from their dilemma. There is not the slightest doubt that every member from the west who votes for this adjournment merely to help this discredited government will have to account for that act to the people of the west. Every Progressive member who votes against the amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre will likewise have to account to his constituents, and I for one would not like to be in his boots when he comes to do so. What possible reason can there be to maintain in office a government that many of the hon. gentlemen to my left, have declared they have no confidence in, and which itself has announced its impotence and inability to carry on? What possible purpose can there be in delaying the ousting of that government from office? If only the hon. members from the west had realized from the start that they are only wasting time in keeping this government in power, and that the sooner they put a Conservative government in power the sooner we could get on with the business of the country-there can be only one outcome to the situation- we could now be proceeding with public business under the leadership of a man possessing the courage to attack the problems awaiting solution, whose integrity no man can doubt, and who has a well-defined policy of his own and the backing of a loyal party from one end of Canada to the other.
I ask hon. members who belong to the Progressive party to consider carefully the result of an adverse vote on this amendment. I believe they would be serving the cause of Canada as a whole by voting for this amendment and against the resolution for an adjournment. I come from Manitoba, and I tell this House that that province in the past has refused baits dangled before it in the shape of local advantage when the interests of Canada as a whole were threatened. Manitoba to-day stands for a sturdier Canadianism. a Canadianism finer than that advocated by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) in his recent speeches here. The voice of

Manitoba calls upon all parts of Canada to unite and to put an end to divisions between provinces and different classes in this country. That is a work in which we should all be proud to engage. Let us all unite in that task so that as members of the Dominion parliament we may have the privilege of giving effect to the boast of Sir Wilfrid Laurier that the twentieth century belongs to Canada. Mr. Speaker, I ask the privilege of saying a very few words in connection with the amendment now before the House. As I understand the situation, we on this side are asked to join with the government in granting an adjournment for six weeks, a demand which I believe, Sir, is without parallel, without precedent and without justification. Perhaps I should qualify the expression "without justification". There is no justification having regard to the good and welfare of the country; the only justification lies in the exigencies of the political fortunes of the so-called Liberal government that we have to-day. Sir, in times of warfare immediately a battle is over the first duty of the commander of every unit that has taken part in the fight is to assemble his forces and to re-form his lines. Well we had a political battle in this country on October 29, and although three and a half months have elapsed since that battle took place, this government have not yet been able to readjust their lines, and we are asked now to grant an adjournment of six weeks in order that they may assemble their forces and carry out that re-forming. What kind of reformers can these people be if they cannot get their line into shape in that time?
But, Sir, it appears that the government have received reinforcements; that the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), in his capacity of commander-in-chief of the Progressive forces, has moved up his men and tried to align them on the side of the government. It -is to 'be hoped that there are still some independents in that so-called Independent group, and that not all the members of the Progressive party will be found subservient to the leadership of my hon. friend. How can the Progressives defend their support of this amendment? Not on the ground of convenience, because taken as a body, no other group in this House will be so much inconvenienced by an adjournment 
as they will, owing to the long distances their homes are from Ottawa. Should an adjournment be granted now, the weeks that will be lost will be tacked on to the far end of the session when time is more important to them than it is at present. Therefore they cannot defend their support of the government on the ground of convenience. Neither can they defend it on the ground of necessity, because so far as they are concerned there is no need or necessity for it. According to my understanding, one of the strong planks of the Progressive platform has always been that of economy, and they cannot endorse an adjournment on that ground. It has been said that this adjournment may cost the country from one hundred thousand to two hundred thousand dollars. If that be so, then if my hon. friends wish to be true to their platform they must oppose the government's proposal. But it appears that there must be some alliance or coalition between the Progressives and Liberals. W'hat the understanding between them is, of course we on this side do not know, but we can safely assume that the old expression "You scratch my back and I will scratch yours" lies at the very foundation of this alliance.
Soon after the first vote had been taken in this House I met a very prominent reformer, whose father had occupied a high position in the Senate on the reform side. In conversation he told me that he regretted the Liberal party had been sustained in the vote in question. He said "I remember well what happened in the province of Ontario twenty-two or twenty-three years ago, when the late Hon. G. W. Ross endeavoured to hold on to power after having lost the confidence of the people. As a reformer I fear that history will repeat itself, and just as the reform party, by reason of Mr. Ross hanging on to power, lost the confidence of the people; just as our party in Ontario, nearly twenty-five years after that happened, is a mere shadow of what it used to be, so too I fear that our party in the Dominion, by reason of our leaders trying to hang on to office after they have been defeated, will leave us in the same unhappy plight, so far as Dominion matters are concerned."
Now, Sir, this government may with the help of the Progressives wiggle through this session.
No chance.

Well, they may wiggle through this session, but if they do, a reckoning is bound to come sooner or later. They must sooner or later submit themselves to the

After the statement made by the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) that he proposed to suggest the appointment of a committee to deal with the question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), I had been expecting to-day that this motion for a committee would have been brought in by the government. But apparently there has been some difficulty in the wording of that motion, and it has not been brought in.
I wish to say that we are not prepared to alter in any way the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre until the motion for this committee has been brought in by the government and passed by the House. At the same time we on this side of the House do not wish to press the government unduly in a matter of this kind, and I rise to move the adjournment of this debate until to-morrow, in the hope that this motion may then be brought in by the government. If this proposal for the adjournment of the debate is not satisfactory to the government, we on this side of the House are prepared to proceed now with a division on the amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre to the motion for the extended adjournment.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
